Good morning to all of you. The 31st Plenary Meeting of the General Assembly is called to order. The Assembly will consider agenda item 65, entitled Report of the Human Rights Council. The documentation under this item is listed in the Journal of the United Nations. I will now make a statement in my capacity as the President of the General Assembly. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, our consideration of the Human Rights Council's report is more than an annual exercise. It is an opportunity to ask whether our collective commitments are making people safer, strengthening their freedoms, and protecting their dignity. I thank the President of the Human Rights Council, who is with us this morning, and all who contribute to this work. Twenty years after its establishment, the Council remains as essential forum for dialogue, scrutiny, and cooperation. Its mechanisms expose violations, bring neglected concerns to international attention, and support Member States in fulfilling their obligations. The report and its addendum bring together the Council’s resolutions, decisions, and presidential statements adopted during the reporting period. These outcomes call for sustained engagement by Member States. But the value of this work cannot be measured by the volume of documents produced. It must be measured by the difference made in people's lives. Excellencies, the theme of the 81st session of the General Assembly is "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All." This places human rights at the heart of our work. Trust grows when rights become reality. And in this regard, allow me to emphasize three priorities. First, let us uphold all human rights for everyone, everywhere, without double standards. Civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights reinforce one another. Freedom from fear and freedom from want belong to the same promise. Dignity cannot be defended selectively. Political disagreement cannot excuse our failure to respond to human suffering and protect human rights. The Universal Periodic Review embodies this principle. Every member state comes before its peers. No country is beyond scrutiny. Every country has something to improve, learn, and contribute. We should therefore approach this process with candor and cooperation and turn recommendations into national actions. Accountability and cooperation are not competing objectives. Both are essential for effective protection. Second, let us connect our institutions more closely to the people they serve. Respecting distinct mandates, we need to strengthen coordination across United Nations human rights, development, peace, and humanitarian work. Early warnings should prompt timely attention. Findings will inform decisions. Commitments will lead to action. Civil society, national human rights institutions, women, young people, and affected communities must help shape that response. Participation is not an accessory to multilateralism, it's the foundation of its legitimacy. For refugees, migrants, and communities facing discrimination, coordination must mean fewer protection gaps, clearer responsibility, and support that arrives in time. Third, we should manage transformation without weakening protection. Reform must make United Nations more effective, responsive, and accountable. Efficiency matters, but savings alone cannot define success. Human rights mandates need adequate, predictable resources. We cannot demand stronger protection while weakening the means to provide it. We should also strengthen the means of implementation at country level. For developing countries, especially those facing severe capacity constraints, commitments must be matched by accessible technical assistance, institutional capacity building, and sustained international cooperation. Support should respond to national priorities, helping translate recommendations into laws, policies, and service. Financing capable institutions and effective partnerships must close the distance between international commitments and daily experience. Transformation also requires us to confront technological change. Artificial intelligence can expand knowledge, services, and opportunity. It can also deepen discrimination and enable intrusive surveillance. Human rights must guide innovation from design to deployment. Developing countries need both the capacity to benefit and a voice in shaping the rules. Decisions affecting everyone cannot be shaped by only a few. Excellencies, the people we serve do not experience our work as separate agendas. They experience safety or insecurity, inclusion or exclusion, opportunity or deprivation. Our response must be equally connected. This debate should strengthen the link between Council’s work and our responsibility to act. Its outcomes must reach beyond our meeting rooms to the institutions and communities where rights are upheld or denied every day. Let us uphold principles consistently, equip institutions adequately, and turn recommendations into protection. This is how we restore trust. This is how we deliver for all. I thank you. In accordance with resolution 65/281, I now give the floor to His Excellency Sidhartho Reza Suryadipuro, President of the Human Rights Council. You have the floor, Mr. President.
Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished Representatives, It is an honor for me, in fulfillment of my mandate as President of the Human Rights Council, to present the Council’s annual report and its addendum. Presenting this report expresses the relationship between the Council and the Assembly, that the Assembly had created 20 years ago as its subsidiary body and to which the Council remains accountable. The General Assembly reaffirmed this relationship in its resolution 80/287. Mr. President, distinguished representative, I turn first to the work of the Council. This year began under severe constraint faced by the entire United Nations system. The extraordinary modalities adopted in 2025, which reduced the Council's meeting by 10%, continue to apply throughout this year. Under these circumstances, in its three regular sessions, the Council adopted 100 resolutions, welcomed 110 dignitaries to its high-level segment, and held 18 panel discussions. The Council addressed for the first time the rights of persons in street situations, children's access to nutritious food, and the human rights dimension of neglected tropical diseases. On technology, two new resolutions addressed the human rights implications of artificial intelligence and the rights of women and girls in the digital sphere. Technical assistance and capacity building remained an important part of the Council's work. A new resolution provided for cooperation with Portuguese-speaking States. The Council's resolutions continued to combine requests for practical assistance with sustained attention to the situations in countries across different regions. The Council responded to urgent developments at its 39th special session. It considered the situation of human rights in the Islamic Republic of Iran in the context of nationwide protests. It held three urgent debates. at its 61st session, on the military aggression launched by the Islamic Republic of Iran against seven states in the region and on the aerial attack on the Shajareh Tayyibe Girls School in Minab, Iran; and at its 62nd session, on the situation in and around Olobeit, Sudan. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, I turn next to the Council's mechanisms and to the participation on which they depend. The Universal Periodic Review remains a central expression of the Council's universal mandate. Through constructive dialogue on an equal footing, each review identifies progress, challenges, and opportunities for cooperation. In decision 63/118, The Council called on a State under review to resume engagement after continued non-cooperation. As the fourth cycle nears its end, I invite Member States to strengthen implementation of recommendations and sustain the cooperation that underpins the mechanism's universality. The Special Procedures and Investigative Bodies bring independent expertise to thematic and country situations that demand sustained attention. Their wealth of information is also an independent source of knowledge on human rights worldwide. Reflecting the Council’s collective and institutional wish, I reaffirm my full support for mandate-holders, whose integrity, independence, and protection from personal attacks, threats, and intimidation are essential to their work. I encourage States and all stakeholders to safeguard them. The Council's work benefits from the participation of the widest possible range of States. The Voluntary Technical Assistance Trust Fund helps address obstacles faced by small island developing States and least developing countries by supporting participation in the Council's sessions. I thank States that support the Fund and encourage continued voluntary contributions. Virtual participation modalities can also help overcome barriers faced by small delegations and civil society, and the Council’s request that this Assembly consider authorizing them as a complement to in-person participation remains before you. I trust there is room to accommodate specific needs of UN organs and in this case, the Human Rights Council. Accessibility is equally integral to meaningful participation, and the Council has requested an advisory committee study on remaining accessibility gaps and practical measures to address them. Mr. President, distinguished representatives, the UN system-wide financial constraints have affected the Council's ability to deliver its programme of work. We must therefore ensure complementarity among our mechanisms and avoid unnecessary overlaps. Under a dedicated track on rationalization and efficiency, delegations in Geneva have worked to streamline a number of mandated reports to the Council and to this Assembly. ended one special procedure mandate, merged resolutions, and moved texts to triennial cycles. These efforts have helped moderate new resource requirements, now at the lowest in more than a decade. My co-facilitators on this track have highlighted a checklist for delegations when they formulate new resolutions, including budget implications, impacts on the programme of work, overlap with existing mandates, sunset clauses, frequency of resolutions, and streamlining of texts. The Human Rights Council is therefore making concrete contribution to the General Assembly-wide mandate review undertaking. The Council has also developed the Human Rights Council Mapper, which, though not yet complete, provides a searchable, evidence-based overview of more than 1,000 texts and 3,000 mandated activities, helping delegations identify overlaps, reporting cycles, and resource implications before decisions are taken. Predictability of financing is particularly important for the Council's work. Financial uncertainty risks disrupting continuity and undermining implementation, even when there's a clear mandate and agreement on the way forward. I therefore urge this Assembly, through its relevant committees, to further lend its support in this regard. Just a week ago, a retreat of the Human Rights Council was held in Bali, Indonesia, hosted by the government of Indonesia, where representatives of states gathered to review the current challenges of the human rights architecture and to explore ways forward. It was not only the farthest retreat ever convened by the President of the Council, it also held extensive discussion about the breadth of the indivisibility of human rights and the need to further bring the Council closer to the ground. National human rights institutions are part of the answer. Their contribution to our work is indispensable. They support follow-up at the national level, bring information and perspective from grassroots communities, and help connect deliberations in Geneva with life lived experience. I invite continued attention to leveraging their role in our deliberations. Regional human rights and regional organizations, for their part, are also important partners. The Council has encouraged them to strengthen cooperation with the United Nations and with another to help translate universal standards to regional and national action. Let me also at this stage acknowledge the important role of civil society organizations. I encourage states to preserve the space for their safe and substantive participation. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, I turn finally to the recommendations of the Council that was placed before you. Resolution 61/7 recommends that this Assembly mark the 60th anniversary of the adoption of the International Covenants during its 81st session. The anniversary offers an opportunity to reaffirm the equal importance of all human rights. In resolution 61/23, the Council invited the Assembly to consider a resolution for a high-level event marking the Genocide Convention's 80th anniversary in 2028, therefore, renewing attention to the prevention and implementation by State Parties. Starting this year, to strengthen coordination and to elevate the work of the Council, this year's Presidency has also extended the practice of sending, after each session, an informal summary of the Council’s substantive discussion, initially addressed to the President of the General Assembly. These letters are now also sent to other relevant United Nations bodies and to regional organizations. Mr. President, distinguished representatives, In this 20th anniversary year of the Council, we can recognize what we have built through two decades of dialogue, scrutiny, and cooperation, while reflecting together on the distance still to travel. My closing message is one that I believe every delegation in this hall can carry. The Human Rights Council is the creation of this Assembly, and it belongs to all of its members. Universality, objectivity, non-selectivity, and the equal treatment of all human rights, including the right to development, remain the guiding principles of our deliberations and of our shared efforts towards tangible improvements in people's lives. We would do well to remember that the strength of the Council lies not only in its ability to respond to human rights challenges, but also in its capacity to foster cooperation and dialogue among Member States with diverse experience and perspectives. It is also a time to pursue consolidation at every layer, between United Nations bodies, between the branches of the Secretariat, and among Member States, including between their own delegations in New York and in Geneva. Together, this may be our most important contributions to the future of multilateralism. Allow me finally to conclude by thanking the General Assembly for its support. I am grateful to the Council's members and observers, the High Commissioner and his office, the Bureau, the national human rights institutions and civil society, the mandate holders, and the United Nations Office in Geneva. It is an honour to present the Council's report to this Assembly, and I look forward to our continued cooperation in fulfilling the mandate entrusted to the Human Rights Council and the determination of the United Nations to, inter alia, reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights and in the dignity and worth of the human person. Thank you.
I thank His Excellency Siddhartha Reza Suryadipuro for his statement as President of the Human Rights Council. Before proceeding further, I propose that the time limits for statements in this debate be five minutes for individual delegations speaking in their national capacity and seven minutes for statements made on behalf of a group of States. I see no objection to this proposal. It is so decided. I now invite Her Excellency Katuna Tlatlazade for a Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs of Georgia to make a statement. You have the floor, madam.
Mr. President, allow me to express my gratitude to the President of the Human Rights Council, Ambassador Suryadipuro, for presenting the annual report. As we mark the 20th anniversary of the Council's establishment, full implementation of its mandate remains as important as ever. We underline the value of the UPR mechanism as a key element of the Council to assess the human rights situation in each country. Georgia underwent its fourth review in January this year. We will spare no effort to ensure implementation of accepted recommendations. Georgia supports inclusive participation by all member states in the Council's work, including throughout its voluntary contributions to the Trust Fund. Excellencies. Let me avail myself of this opportunity to thank all delegations that supported and co-sponsored the resolution, "Cooperation with Georgia," adopted by consensus for the second consecutive year. We believe that maintaining this consolidated stance is vital in addressing the deteriorating human rights and humanitarian situation in Abkhazia and Tshinvali regions of Georgia, occupied by the Russian Federation.
The resolution reiterates the call for immediate and unimpeded access.
For the Office of High Commissioner for Human Rights and international and regional human rights mechanisms to occupied regions of Georgia. Regrettably, such access continues to be denied by the Russian Federation. Distinguished delegates, the human rights situation in the occupied regions of Georgia remains deeply concerning. The population continues to face arbitrary detentions, restrictions on freedom of movement, closure of so-called crossing points, violation of property rights, torture, treatment, and systematic ethnic discrimination, including restrictions on education in the Georgian language. Unfortunately, no meaningful progress has been made towards ensuring the safe and dignified return of hundreds of thousands of internally displaced persons and refugees to their homes. In this context, international engagement and accountability remain indispensable. The European Court of Human Rights and the International Criminal Court have confirmed that the Russian Federation, as the power exercising effective control over the occupied regions, bears full responsibility for all human rights violations committed therein.
Mr. President, the Russian Federation continues to disregard the EU The 2008 ceasefire agreement of 12 August 2008 and its policy.
Aimed at further integrating the occupied regions of Georgia with the ultimate objective of their de facto annexation. In this regard, let me stress the recent alarming developments: so-called presidential elections held in the occupied Tskhinvali region on 18 September 2026; operation of Russian State Duma polling stations in both occupied regions without the consent of the Government of Georgia; recent so-called.
And appointments with further deepened administrative control over the Tskhinvali region by the Russian Federation.
At the same time, Georgia remains deeply concerned about the devastating human rights consequences of Russia's ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine and the continuing violations of international law. We reaffirm our unwavering support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, including its territorial waters.
And support the Council's continued efforts to ensure accountability and justice. In conclusion, Georgia will continue to contribute to the work of the Council and to strengthen the international human rights system.
We call on the international community to remain united in upholding international law, ensuring accountability for grave human rights violations, and protecting the rights of all individuals.
I thank you, madam, for your statement. And I now call upon European Union to speak on behalf of the EU and its member states.
Mr. President, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states. The candidate countries Montenegro, Albania, the Republic of Moldova, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as Andorra and San Marino, align themselves with this statement. We thank Ambassador Sirin Dipuro for presenting the annual report and for your leadership of the Human Rights Council. Colleagues, we meet at a difficult time. War and conflict continue to claim lives and devastate communities. Around the world, human rights violations, democratic backsliding, and restrictions on civil space threaten hard-won progress. And these challenges are interconnected; one affects the other. The Human Rights Council cannot resolve these challenges alone, but it has an essential role in providing early warning, ensuring that human rights violations are documented, and that victims are heard, thereby contributing to fighting impunity, promoting accountability, and preventing future violations and abuses. This year marks 20 years since the Human Rights Council held its first session. Over these two decades, The Council has been a vital forum, the vital forum, for dialogue, cooperation, technical assistance, and has developed important instruments to advance its mandate to promote and protect human rights worldwide. The Universal Periodic Review brings every state's human rights record under scrutiny and advises on how to improve it. The Special Procedures provide independent expertise and early warning. investigative mechanisms help establish facts and preserve evidence. These mechanisms are complementary, but their value ultimately depends on whether states implement their recommendations and abide by their human rights obligations. During the past year, the EU and its member states have worked with partners across regions on initiatives in the Council that address the full range of human rights. We supported several resolutions on economic, social, and cultural rights, including the right to education, to adequate housing, to access to safe drinking water and sanitation. We led the work on the resolution on freedom of religion and belief, and supported several other resolutions on civil and political rights, including on freedom of opinion and expression, countering disinformation, and efforts to combat torture and enforced disappearances. We continue to promote gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls, the rights of children, youth, older persons, indigenous peoples, and persons with disabilities, as well as the fight against racism and protection of human rights defenders and civic space. And we also led and supported initiatives addressing the human rights implications of artificial intelligence and digital technologies, ensuring that technological progress respects human rights and fundamental freedoms. Across these areas, we recognize the importance of cooperation and inclusive dialogue. President, the EU continues to protect and promote human rights both at home and abroad. We recognize that no country has an ideal human rights record, and that we all have work to do. For our part, we remain open to constructive criticism, dialogue, and learning from others. This includes cooperating fully with the UN human rights mechanisms. All 27 EU member states have issued a standing invitation to the UN special procedures. We urge others to do the same. The Universal Periodic Review is a unique tool, and we must continue to safeguard it as a credible, inclusive, universal, and effective mechanism that enjoys the participation of all States.
